title: Feedback & Correction — The Deep Dive

pts: Give learners the first chance to self-correct — often they already know and simply slipped.
Peer correction next builds a habit of attentive listening and shared responsibility for accuracy.
Teacher correction is the last resort, not the default first move.

items: When a learner makes an error during accuracy practice, first signal that something is wrong without saying what (a raised eyebrow, a finger gesture, repeating up to the error).
Wait. Give the learner three to five seconds to self-correct.
If they cannot, invite a peer: ‘Who can help?’
If no one can, give the correct form yourself, clearly and briefly.
Return to the first learner and ask them to say the whole sentence correctly.
Agree a set of finger signals with the class: one finger for a wrong word, two fingers held apart for a missing word.
In writing, the equivalent is to mark the location of the error and ask the learner to fix it (point 4).
Support: for very anxious learners, skip the peer stage and give the correct form quietly.
Stretch: ask the peer to explain why, not just give the answer.

lines: S1: Yesterday I go to the temple.
T: Yesterday I… ? [rising intonation, pause]
S1: …went. Yesterday I went to the temple.
T: Good.
T: Who can help Arjun?
S2: Went.
T: Thank you. Arjun, the whole sentence?
S1: Yesterday I went to the temple.

body: Purpose: to show the order of correction. Content: three stacked steps, like a small staircase. Bottom step, largest: ‘Self-correction (first chance)’, with a single figure thinking. Middle step: ‘Peer correction (second chance)’, with two figures. Top step, smallest: ‘Teacher correction (last resort)’, with a teacher figure. An arrow shows movement upward only when needed. Style: simple, friendly, three colours. Board version: three boxes stacked.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in). Record learners doing an accuracy task; play back and let them self-correct from the recording.

blocks.x: Agreed hand signals, as in the variations.

points.sub: Match correction to the task's goal
pts: Correct immediately during accuracy-focused controlled practice, where precision is the point.
Delay correction until after fluency tasks, so communication isn't interrupted mid-flow.
Announce which mode you're in — learners correct differently when they know what's being prioritised.

items: Make two signs and put them at the top of the board.
Before each activity, point to one sign and say what it means for correction.
In accuracy mode, correct immediately using the hierarchy (point 1).
In fluency mode, do not interrupt; note errors for later.
After a fluency task, spend three to five minutes on delayed feedback.
At the end of the week, ask learners which mode helps them most and why.
Use coloured cards: green for fluency (‘go’), orange for accuracy (‘careful’).
Let learners choose the mode for some tasks.
Support: learners who are anxious may prefer fluency mode more often at first.
Stretch: in accuracy mode, ask learners to self-monitor and correct their own speech.

lines: This is accuracy time. I will stop you and help you when there’s a mistake.
This is fluency time. Just talk. I will listen and we’ll talk about language afterwards.

blocks.x: Delayed feedback after fluency work draws on your monitoring notes (Unit 7): four good examples, four to fix.

body: Purpose: to show the mode signs. Content: two traffic-sign-style signs side by side. Left: an orange diamond labelled ‘ACCURACY’ with a small icon of a magnifying glass and the words ‘Stop and fix’. Right: a green circle labelled ‘FLUENCY’ with an icon of a speech bubble and the words ‘Keep going’. Style: bold, poster-like. Board version: two words at the top of the board.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version). Show the mode as a large text label on screen during each activity.

blocks.x: Printed signs attached to the board with tape.

pts: A recast reformulates the learner's error correctly without flagging it as a mistake.
Recasts are low-threat but are frequently not even noticed as correction by the learner.
Explicit correction is unambiguous but can be face-threatening if used too often or too publicly.
points.who: Roy Lyster's research on recasts in the classroom

v: 20 minutes (in a training session or self-study)
Transcript extracts; a recording of your own lesson

items: Read the examples in the model language. Label each feedback move: recast, clarification request, repetition, metalinguistic clue, elicitation, explicit correction.
Discuss: which moves give the learner a chance to self-correct?
Record five minutes of your own lesson and list your feedback moves.
Count how often each type appears and how often learners repaired their error afterwards.
Plan to use more prompts (moves that push learners to self-correct) in accuracy work next week.
In pairs, role-play teacher and learner, trying each feedback type.
Observe a colleague and note learner uptake after each move.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Types of oral feedback (after Lyster and Ranta 1997):

lines: Recast: S: She go to school. T: She goes to school, yes.
Explicit correction: T: Not ‘go’. We say ‘goes’.
Clarification request: T: Sorry?
Repetition: T: She go? [rising intonation]
Metalinguistic clue: T: Remember, he, she, it…
Elicitation: T: She…?

blocks.x: Recasts are gentle and keep conversation flowing, but learners often do not notice them as correction. Prompts (clarification, repetition, clues, elicitation) push learners to produce the correct form themselves.

body: Purpose: to position feedback types on a continuum. Content: a horizontal line from ‘implicit’ (left) to ‘explicit’ (right). Along it, six labelled markers in order: recast, clarification request, repetition, elicitation, metalinguistic clue, explicit correction. Above the middle four, a bracket labelled ‘prompts: learner does the repair’. Style: clean continuum, one accent colour for the bracket. Board version: a line with six words.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in) for recording your own lessons.

blocks.x: Ask a colleague to sit in for ten minutes and tally your feedback moves on a sheet.

pts: Direct feedback supplies the correct form; indirect feedback marks the error's location and lets the learner fix it.
Indirect feedback generally produces more durable learning because it demands active problem-solving.
The Truscott–Ferris debate remains open on how much correction actually improves subsequent writing.
points.who: John Truscott's critique of correction; Dana Ferris's rebuttal

v: Three short pieces of learner writing; a correction code

items: Introduce a simple correction code (see model language).
Return a piece of writing with errors underlined and coded, not corrected.
Learners correct their own errors, using the code, notes and dictionaries.
In pairs, they check each other’s corrections.
The teacher checks the revised version and gives direct correction only for errors learners could not fix.
Learners note in their error log (point 8) which errors they could and could not fix.
For lower levels, use fewer code symbols (three or four).
Try comparing classes: one gets direct correction, the other coded; test both classes on a new piece of writing.
Support: give direct correction for errors beyond the learner’s current level.
Stretch: underline without coding, so learners must diagnose the error type.

lines: T = tense / WW = wrong word / Sp = spelling / ^ = something missing / WO = word order / P = punctuation
Direct: Yesterday I ~~go~~ went to the market.
Indirect (coded): Yesterday I go (T) to the market.

blocks.x: The debate: Truscott (1996) argued that grammar correction in writing is ineffective and may be harmful; Ferris (1999) and later studies argued that focused, clear correction can help. Bitchener and Ferris (2012) summarize the research since.

body: Purpose: to show what coded feedback looks like. Content: a short handwritten paragraph by a learner on lined paper. Several words are underlined, with small code letters in the margin (T, WW, ^, Sp). A box in the corner shows the code key. Style: realistic but tidy handwriting, one colour of teacher ink (not red). Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). Use ‘Suggesting’ mode for direct correction or add comments with code letters for indirect correction.
Write & Improve (Cambridge, free with registration). Automated feedback highlights areas that may need attention; learners decide how to fix them.

blocks.x: Pencil codes in the margin. Many teachers avoid red ink, which learners often associate with failure.

pts: Focused feedback targets one error type across a piece of writing or speech.
Unfocused feedback — marking every error at once — overwhelms and rarely leads to lasting change.
Rotate the focus across drafts or lessons so different error types each get concentrated attention.

items: Choose one error type that is frequent and important for the class (for example, articles).
Tell learners in advance: ‘This time I will only mark a, an and the.’
Mark only that error type throughout the piece.
Learners correct those errors and write a short rule in their own words.
On the next piece of writing, choose a different focus, but ask learners to check the previous one themselves.
Rotate focuses through a term: tenses, articles, prepositions, sentence boundaries.
Let learners choose their own focus from their error log.
Support: choose a focus with a clear rule (third-person -s).
Stretch: choose a focus requiring judgement (articles, prepositions).

blocks.x: Unfocused and focused feedback on the same sentence:

lines: Unfocused: every error marked in a single piece of work. Learners may feel overwhelmed and fix nothing.
Focused (articles only): I saw ^ elephant near the temple. The elephant was eating ~~a~~ bananas.

body: Figure 8.5 A spotlight on one error type

Purpose: to show focused feedback visually. Content: a page of writing in shadow, with a circular spotlight falling on three highlighted articles. Beside it, the same page covered in marks of many colours, labelled ‘everything at once’. Style: contrasting, clear. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs comments filtered by a label (such as ‘[A]’ for articles) so learners can find all comments of one type.

blocks.x: A single-colour pencil used only for the week’s focus.

body: Tell learners which error type you are focusing on before they write, not after. They will check for it while writing, which is often more valuable than any correction you add afterwards.

pts: Over-correction, especially in front of peers, raises anxiety and can suppress a learner's willingness to speak at all.
A high affective filter is argued to block input from being processed for acquisition, regardless of its quality.
Calibrate correction frequency to the learner's confidence, not only to the density of their errors.

v: 5 minutes at the end of a lesson, once a week

items: At the end of the lesson, give each learner a slip with two questions: ‘Did you speak English today? How did you feel about being corrected?’
Learners answer with a face or a few words, anonymously.
After class, read the slips. Look for signs that correction is discouraging speaking.
Adjust: more fluency mode, more private correction, more praise for attempts.
Repeat each week for a month and compare.
Ask ‘What helps you when you make a mistake?’ and use the answers to set class norms.
For teenagers, ask whether they prefer correction in front of the class or privately.
Support: allow answers in a home language.
Stretch: learners suggest a correction rule for the class.

blocks.x: Class norms for mistakes, agreed with learners:

lines: Mistakes are how we learn. We don’t laugh at mistakes. The teacher corrects kindly and briefly. We try to fix our own mistakes first.

blocks.x: The affective filter (Krashen 1982): anxiety and low confidence may act as a filter that blocks input from being processed. Correction that raises anxiety can therefore work against learning, even when it is accurate.

body: Purpose: to explain the idea simply. Content: a stream of words (input) flowing towards a learner’s head. Between them, a mesh filter. On the left, the filter is thick and dark (labelled ‘high anxiety’) and few words pass through. On the right, the filter is thin and light (labelled ‘low anxiety’) and many words pass. Style: simple, calm colours. Board version: two filters drawn as grids of different density.

items: Google Forms (free), anonymous, with a face-scale question.

blocks.x: Slips in a box by the door.

body: Research on foreign language anxiety (Horwitz, Horwitz and Cope 1986) found that it is a distinct kind of anxiety, tied to using a language in front of others, and that it can affect capable learners as much as weaker ones. A quiet learner is not necessarily a learner who knows little.

pts: Specific, process-focused praise ('good use of the past perfect there') supports motivation better than a generic 'good job.'
Praise tied to effort and strategy use encourages a growth mindset toward language learning.
Empty praise, given too often, loses its informational value and stops functioning as feedback at all.

items: For one week, notice your usual praise words (Good. Very good. Excellent.).
Replace some with specific praise: say what was good and why.
Praise strategies and effort as well as results.
Occasionally ask a learner to say what they did well.
Note learners’ reactions. Does specific praise lead to more attempts?
Written praise: one specific positive comment on every piece of writing before any correction.
Peer praise: learners give one specific compliment to a partner after a speaking task.
Support: for learners who rarely succeed, praise small, specific steps.
Stretch: for strong learners, praise risk-taking with new language.

lines: Generic: Good job.
Specific: You used because to give a reason. That made your opinion much clearer.
Strategy praise: You checked your verbs before handing it in. It shows: all your past forms are correct.
Effort praise: You tried a new word, crowded, even though you weren’t sure. That’s how you learn.

body: Purpose: a desk card. Content: four speech bubbles, each with a sentence frame: ‘You used ___ to ___.’, ‘I liked the way you ___.’, ‘Your ___ is much better than last time.’, ‘You tried ___. Keep doing that.’ Style: bright, simple. Board version: not applicable.

items: ClassDojo (free). Some teachers use it to record positive behaviour; if you use it, make the recorded feedback specific rather than just points. [Check school policy on data privacy before use with children.]

blocks.x: Written comments on a sticky note attached to the learner’s notebook.

pts: A running, learner-specific error log turns scattered correction into a long-term diagnostic record.
Patterns across weeks reveal which errors are genuinely fossilising versus which were one-off slips.
Review the log periodically with the learner — it becomes part of the ongoing needs analysis from Unit 2.

v: 10 minutes to set up; 5 minutes weekly
A page at the back of each notebook

items: Learners rule a page with four columns: date, my sentence, correct sentence, rule or reminder.
Each time an error is corrected (orally or in writing), the learner adds it.
Every two weeks, learners read their log and circle errors that appear more than once.
The teacher collects logs once a month and notes class-wide patterns.
Use the patterns to plan focused feedback (point 5) and language focus stages.
A shared class log of ‘common mistakes this month’ on the wall.
A digital log in a spreadsheet.
Support: the teacher writes the first few entries with the learner.
Stretch: learners add a new example sentence for each rule.

lines: 12 Sept / I am agree. / I agree. / agree is a verb; no am.
The same error across many learners → whole-class focus.
The same error in one learner, repeatedly → possible fossilization (Unit 6), individual plan.
An error that disappears → learning has happened; say so to the learner.

body: Purpose: a photocopiable template. Content: an A4 page with four ruled columns (Date, My sentence, Correct sentence, Rule/reminder) and a small box at the bottom, ‘Errors I no longer make’. Style: clean, ruled, 10 pt headings. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A personal error log with a column for error type; learners can sort to see their most frequent types.

blocks.x: The notebook page, as in the activity.

body: Ask each learner to count the entries in their error log that they no longer make. Celebrate the number. Seeing errors disappear is one of the most convincing forms of progress a learner can experience.

dek: Unit 8 of 100: who should correct, when, and how — from the self-correction hierarchy to written feedback that actually improves the next draft.

aims.x: This unit examines how to respond to learners’ errors and successes so that feedback actually changes what they do next. It covers who corrects, when, how directly, how much, and with what effect on confidence.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: use a self–peer–teacher hierarchy of correction;
decide when to correct immediately and when to delay;
choose between recasts, prompts and explicit correction;
give direct and indirect written feedback and know the debate around it;
focus feedback on one error type at a time;
protect learners’ willingness to speak while still correcting;
give specific, process-focused praise;
set up and use error logs as long-term diagnostic records.

why: Why this matters. Feedback is one of the highest-leverage tools a teacher has — and one of the easiest to deploy in ways that quietly discourage the learners it's meant to help.

background.x: Few things a teacher does are as frequent, or as consequential, as responding to what learners say and write. A single lesson may contain dozens of moments of feedback: a nod, a repeated word with rising intonation, a red circle, a ‘Good!’. Each one carries information, and each one also carries a message about how the teacher sees the learner.

The research on feedback is large and not always tidy. John Hattie and Helen Timperley’s review of educational feedback across subjects (2007) found it to be one of the most powerful influences on learning, but also found that some kinds of feedback make things worse, especially praise or criticism aimed at the person rather than at the task. In language learning specifically, Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta (1997) observed that the most common form of oral correction in the classrooms they studied, the recast, was the least likely to lead learners to repair their own errors. In writing, John Truscott (1996) argued provocatively that grammar correction does more harm than good, and Dana Ferris (1999) replied that the question is not whether to correct but how.

The picture that emerges is not a single rule but a set of principles. Give learners the first chance to correct themselves. Match correction to the purpose of the activity. Focus on a few things at a time. Make feedback specific, and connect it to what learners can do next. And watch its effect on confidence, because a learner who has stopped speaking can no longer be corrected at all.

items: Self-correction rate. In an accuracy task, tally how many errors learners corrected themselves after a prompt. Compare over a term.
Uptake after written feedback. Compare errors in a first and a revised draft to see which feedback learners could act on.
Error log trends. Monthly review of class logs: are the most frequent errors changing?
Confidence slips. Track the proportion of positive responses to ‘How did you feel about being corrected?’
Which feedback moves do you use most? Which of them give learners the chance to correct themselves?
How do learners in your class react to being corrected in front of others?
When you mark writing, do you correct everything? What would change if you focused on one error type?
What words do you use when you praise? How specific are they?
Which errors do you see year after year? What might you do differently about them?

terms.def: Krashen’s (1982) metaphor for emotional states such as anxiety or low confidence that block input from being acquired; a relaxed, supportive classroom is said to lower the filter.
A move asking a speaker to repeat or explain what they said, such as ‘Sorry, what do you mean?’; it serves both negotiation of meaning and implicit error correction.
A set of symbols used to mark types of error in writing, such as T for tense, so that learners can correct their own mistakes.
A sequence of correction moves, from least to most explicit, that gives learners the chance to self-correct before the teacher supplies the correct form.
Correcting errors after an activity has finished rather than during it, so that learners can focus on fluency and communication.

Corrective feedback in which the teacher supplies the correct form, for example by crossing out goed and writing went above it. It is quick and clear, and useful when learners cannot yet correct the error themselves.

Drawing language, ideas or answers out of learners through questions, prompts, pictures or gestures instead of simply telling them. As corrective feedback, it prompts learners to self-correct, for example ‘Yesterday I…?’
A record kept by the learner of their own errors, usually in three columns: what I wrote or said, the correct version, and my rule or reminder. It supports self-monitoring and learner autonomy.
Corrective feedback that targets one or a few selected error types, such as past tense forms, rather than every error in a piece of work. It is usually easier for learners to act on.
The worry and nervousness specific to using or learning a foreign language, such as fear of speaking in front of others or of negative evaluation (Horwitz, Horwitz and Cope 1986).
Corrective feedback that shows an error has been made, for example by underlining or using a code, without supplying the correct form, so that learners correct it themselves.
Corrective feedback that comments on or asks about the form of an error without supplying the correct form, such as ‘Past tense?’ or ‘Is that a countable noun?’ (Lyster and Ranta 1997).
Learners correcting one another’s errors, often after a teacher prompt; it encourages attention to form and keeps more learners involved.
1. In error correction, a move that pushes the learner to self-correct, such as a clarification request or metalinguistic clue. 2. In generative AI, the instruction or question typed to the system.

Corrective feedback in which the teacher reformulates all or part of a learner’s incorrect utterance correctly, without explicitly signalling the error (Lyster and Ranta 1997). For example, learner: ‘He go yesterday’; teacher: ‘Oh, he went yesterday?’

A learner correcting their own error, often after a prompt from the teacher such as a repeated word, a questioning look or a gesture. Self-correction encourages learners to notice and apply what they already know.

Praise that names exactly what a learner did well, such as ‘You used three linking words in that paragraph’, rather than a general ‘Good’. It tells learners what to repeat and builds realistic confidence.
A learner’s immediate response to corrective feedback, such as repeating or correcting the form (Lyster and Ranta 1997). Uptake shows that feedback was noticed, but does not in itself prove learning.
